lead: Laser engineered net shaping (LENS) builds metal by melting powder that is flying through the air, not powder lying in a bed. A laser makes a small melt pool on a solid metal substrate; a nozzle blows alloy powder into that same pool. The pool freezes behind the moving beam as a track, and track over track makes a layer. LENS is the best-known member of directed energy deposition (DED). Shops use it to repair worn shafts and turbine parts, to clad a cheap base with a hard surface, and to build near-net metal shapes that are later machined.
prereq: You need: the powder bed picture in Chapter 7.5 and the laser melt pool of laser welding in Unit 4, Laser welding.

sections.h3: A melt pool fed by blown powder

blocks.text: A focused laser beam strikes a solid metal surface and forms a small molten pool, a few millimetres across. Metal powder is blown down a nozzle into that same pool. The powder grains melt as they arrive, the pool grows, and the motion system drags the pool along the surface. The liquid metal left behind freezes into a track.

Nothing sits in a bed. A powder grain exists only for the fraction of a second between the nozzle and the pool. Grains that miss the pool fly past and are collected for reuse, so the powder you feed is never the powder you deposit.

LENS belongs to a family called directed energy deposition (DED): energy and material are delivered to the same point at the same time. Some syllabi use the names laser cladding, laser metal deposition or direct metal deposition for the same family. LENS is a trade name that entered textbooks. All of them share one physics: a moving melt pool fed with blown powder or wire.

blocks.where: V̇ is deposited volume per hour (cm³/h); ṁ is the powder mass feed rate (g/h); ρ is the alloy density (g/cm³); η is the catchment efficiency, the fraction of blown powder that actually enters the pool (a number below 1, set by nozzle alignment and beam focus).

blocks.text: An inert gas such as argon does two jobs: it carries the powder out of the nozzle and it shields the hot metal from oxygen. Titanium and nickel alloys react badly with air at these temperatures, so the shield gas is not optional.

items: Clamp the substrate, or the worn part being repaired, flat under the head and set the nozzle height.
Set laser power, spot diameter, scan speed, powder feed rate and shield gas flow.
Deposit the first track slowly; the pool must wet the substrate and bond to it.
Step sideways by the hatch spacing, about half the track width, and run the next track in the reverse direction.
On finishing a layer, raise the head by one layer height and repeat the scan pattern.
Cool, unclamp, stress relieve, then machine the rough surface to final size.

blocks.text: Typical numbers: laser power from a few hundred watts to a few kilowatts, track width about 0.5 mm to 3 mm, layer height about 0.2 mm to 1 mm, powder grains a few tens of micrometres across. Small spot and low powder rate give a finer track but a slower build.

The deposit is rough and slightly oversized, so every functional surface is machined afterwards. Residual stresses build up because each new track shrinks as it cools against metal that is already solid.

items: Repair: a worn shaft, a damaged turbine blade root or a cracked die is built back up only where metal is missing, then machined to size. The part itself is the substrate.
Cladding: a hard or corrosion-resistant alloy such as a cobalt or nickel alloy is laid on a cheaper base, for valve seats, pump sleeves and shear blades.
Near-net preforms: a bulky metal shape is deposited close to final size and finished by machining, saving the material lost in cutting from solid.
Materials: carbon and stainless steels, tool steels, titanium alloys such as Ti-6Al-4V, and nickel superalloys such as Inconel 625 and 718.

blocks.text: A hybrid machine mounts the LENS head on a CNC milling spindle, so one setup deposits metal and then mills it flat. This keeps a dimension under control at every layer and removes the rough skin before the next layer goes down.

LENS loses to powder bed fusion where fine detail matters. It cannot build small internal cooling channels, thin lattices or sharp fine features, because the pool is about a millimetre wide and the powder spray spreads wider than that. Its strengths are the opposite ones: large parts, high deposition rate, a substrate that can be an existing component, and no powder bed to fill or clean.

figure.caption: Laser and powder arrive at the same point and form a melt pool, which freezes into a deposited track; the CNC table carries the work away so the next track and the next layer can follow.

spec.title: LENS build
spec.aria: A vertical flow shows a laser and powder nozzle meeting at a melt pool, depositing a track on a CNC table to build or repair a part.

examples.question: A worn shaft of diameter 50 mm and length 100 mm must be built up by 0.5 mm on the radius over its full length using LENS. The machine deposits metal at a volume rate of 20 cm³/h. Find the volume of metal needed and the deposition time in hours and minutes.
steps: Initial radius r₁ = d/2 = 50/2 = 25 mm. Final radius r₂ = 25 + 0.5 = 25.5 mm.
Volume of the built-up sleeve: V = π(r₂² − r₁²) × L.
r₂² = 25.5² = 650.25 mm²; r₁² = 25² = 625 mm²; difference = 25.25 mm².
Time t = V ÷ V̇ = 7.93 cm³ ÷ 20 cm³/h = 0.397 h.
examples.answer: Volume to deposit is 7.93 cm³ and the deposition time is 0.397 h, that is about 23.8 minutes.
examples.check:
import math
d = 50.0
build = 0.5
L = 100.0
rate = 20.0
r1 = d/2
r2 = r1 + build
V_mm3 = math.pi*(r2**2 - r1**2)*L
V_cm3 = V_mm3/1000.0
t_h = V_cm3/rate
t_min = t_h*60
print(round(V_cm3, 2))
print(round(t_h, 3))
print(round(t_min, 1))

traps: Calling LENS a powder bed process. There is no bed, no recoater and no surrounding powder; the powder is blown into the pool and the rest flies past.
Forgetting the substrate. The first track must wet and bond to solid metal, so LENS always needs something to build on, unlike a bed process that starts on a plate under loose powder.
Mixing radial and diametral build-up. A 0.5 mm radial build adds 1 mm to the diameter, so the radius, not the diameter, goes into r₂.
Using feed rate as deposition rate. Powder fed × catchment efficiency is what lands, so the deposited volume rate is always smaller than ṁ ÷ ρ.
Expecting fine internal channels. The pool is about a millimetre wide; small channels and lattices belong to powder bed fusion.

quiz.q: Expand LENS and name the AM family it belongs to.
quiz.a: Laser engineered net shaping. It belongs to directed energy deposition (DED), the blown-powder branch.

quiz.q: Why must a LENS build start on a solid substrate?
quiz.a: The laser needs metal to melt and the liquid pool needs a surface to wet and freeze onto. The substrate also conducts heat away, so the first track solidifies quickly and bonds metallurgically. Without it there is nothing to hold the pool.

quiz.q: A LENS nozzle feeds 300 g/h of steel powder of density 8.0 g/cm³ with a catchment efficiency of 0.6. Find the deposited volume rate.
A single track is 2 mm wide and 0.5 mm high over a length of 100 mm. At a deposition rate of 20 cm³/h, how long does the track take?
A worn 50 mm shaft must be restored. Explain why LENS is a better choice than powder bed fusion here.
quiz.a: The shaft is its own substrate, so it goes straight under the head with no bed to fill around a long part. Only the worn band is built up, so distortion and machining are small, and the shaft can be turned back to size after deposition. Powder bed fusion would need the whole shaft inside a powder bed, which is impractical for a long component and would fuse powder over the entire surface.

quiz.q: A LENS deposit shows porosity and partly melted powder particles stuck to the surface. Give two process causes.
quiz.a: Energy input is too low for the powder feed: laser power too low or scan speed too high, so grains arrive faster than the pool can melt them. Or the powder feed rate is too high for the beam, or the shield gas flow is wrong so the pool oxidises. Fix by raising power, slowing the scan, cutting the feed rate or resetting the nozzle and gas.

quiz.q: State two jobs of the argon stream in LENS.
quiz.a: It carries the powder from the hopper to the nozzle and it shields the melt pool from oxygen, which matters for titanium and nickel alloys.

beyond: Not for the exam. LENS heads now sit on robot arms and on hybrid additive–subtractive machining centres, so a single setup deposits and mills a part. Wire-fed DED, often called wire arc additive manufacturing, trades the powder nozzle for a wire and reaches much higher deposition rates for large frames. Research is pushing in-situ melt pool monitoring with pyrometers and cameras, closed-loop control of layer height, and repair of turbine blades and dies in maintenance shops. Search for directed energy deposition, laser metal deposition, wire arc additive manufacturing and hybrid additive manufacturing to go further.
